Chapter 7: Overcoming Organizational Barriers to Good Choices.
Even when you’ve got individuals and teams who really care about making smart decisions, bigger organizations can throw up some pretty unique hurdles. You know how hierarchies, silos, and old habits can make it tough to question the way things have always been done? Or to try something new? Let’s explore how you can build a culture where everyone—from the front lines to the top—feels empowered to make better choices.
One of the first steps is creating psychological safety. Imagine working somewhere you can speak up, ask tough questions, or even admit you’re unsure—without fear. That feeling doesn’t just show up on its own. Leaders need to set the tone. When someone in charge shows humility, welcomes disagreements, and even thanks people for flagging issues early, it sends a clear message: honest feedback is valued here. For instance, think of a manager who regularly asks, “What are we missing?” or “Who sees this differently?” Those simple questions open the door for new ideas and alternative viewpoints—no one gets shut down just for thinking differently.
Another big move? Make learning part of the routine. After a major project or launch, picture the team gathering not just to celebrate or point fingers, but to unpack what actually happened. What worked? What flopped? What could we do better next time? These after-action reviews help everyone treat mistakes as valuable data, not personal failures. Over time, this shift builds a culture where continuous improvement is just what you do—successes and stumbles both become learning moments.
Now, if you want to break out of the old way of doing things, try starting small. Instead of insisting every new idea needs massive buy-in right away, let teams experiment on a small scale. Maybe a hospital tests out a new check-in process in just one department before rolling it out everywhere. This way, the stakes are lower, the fear of failure drops, and you can actually learn from real-world feedback before committing.
So, what are some practical steps you can take to break through those organizational barriers?
First, foster psychological safety. Leaders should invite tough questions and make it a point to reward people who spot problems early.
Second, institutionalize learning. Make post-decision reviews a regular, expected part of your workflow—not just an afterthought.
Third, encourage small experiments. Give teams the freedom to test new ideas on a small scale before asking everyone to jump on board.
By tackling the structural and cultural factors that shape how choices get made, organizations can become places where smart decisions aren’t just possible—they’re expected. Imagine that: an environment where everyone, at every level, feels like their voice and their ideas truly matter.
